newsitem.title: USA: Publishers sue U.S. agency over First Amendment rights.
newsitem.headline: Publishers sue U.S. agency over First Amendment rights.

text.p: A group of newsletter and book publishers sued the Commodity Futures Trading Commission on Wednesday, charging the agency violates the constitutional right of free speech.
The CFTC hindered free speech rights, they said, by requiring financial publishers and possibly Internet users to register with the agency.
The lawsuit is the latest in a series of legal actions brought by First Amendment advocates concerned about free speech protection on the Internet.

"Unless the CFTC is stopped, those who distribute pornographic pictures over the Internet enjoy more protection than those who want to meet in an on-line chat room to talk about coffee futures and pork bellies," said Scott Bullock, an attorney with the Institute for Justice.
The institute filed the lawsuit in federal court in Washington on behalf of ten publishers and subscribers of commodity books and newsletters.
A spokesman for the CFTC said the agency had not yet seen the lawsuit and had no immediate comment.

The CFTC, which has regulated U.S. commodity traders and brokers for more than two decades, in 1995 began requiring publishers of commodity newsletters, books and publications to register with the agency. The publishers are considered by the agency to be "commodity trading advisors," who sell analyses or reports about commodity futures and options.

Last summer, the CFTC said it planned to expand the rules to include Internet user groups, hyperlinks or web pages that mention commodity trading. The agency abruptly suspended the plan pending further review after opponents said the rule would infringe on the constitutional right of free speech.
Registration with the agency includes providing a set of fingerprints, and complying with CFTC auditors' requests for subscriber names, addresses and other publication records.

Stephen Briese, editor of the Bullish Review newsletter, said he joined the lawsuit out of fear that he could face penalties of five years in jail and a $500,000 fine if he were found to be violating the CFTC regulation. The Bullish Review, published twice a month, analyses CFTC statistical data on large trader commitments and has several hundred subscribers.
"The CFTC has not targeted me or asked me to register," Briese said. "But I'm concerned about the risk of prosecution simply because I publish a newsletter about commodity trading."
Larger publications such as the Wall Street Journal are exempt from the CFTC rule because commodities reporting is not the major thrust of their newsgathering activity, Bullock said.

In 1985, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a similar regulation by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, and found that publishers of "impersonal advice" about stock trading cannot be forced to register with the SEC.
